title: Asymptotically Optimal Circuit Depth for Diagonal Unitary Synthesis and Compilation on Two-Dimensional Grids
authors: Chengzhuo Xu, Xiao Chen, Zhihao Liu, Zhigang Li
abstract: Diagonal unitaries are a fundamental but resource-intensive class of quantum operations, arising as the phase separators of QAOA and the time-evolution blocks of Hamiltonian simulation. Under all-to-all connectivity their optimal depth is established, but on nearest-neighbor hardware general-purpose compilers fall back on heuristic search, which yields no analyzable cost bound and becomes intractable at the very sizes where depth is the bottleneck. We address synthesis and compilation jointly. On the synthesis side, we develop a Gray-Path Framework (GPF) that realizes any $n$-qubit diagonal unitary in asymptotically optimal $R_z$ and CNOT depth $O(2^n/n)$ without ancillas. Our main result is that compiling GPF onto a two-dimensional nearest-neighbor grid preserves this optimality: routing adds depth $Θ(2^n/n)$ and gate count $Θ(2^n)$. Because GPF fixes its entire interaction structure in advance, routing reduces to scheduling a known sequence, with no heuristic search. We give the construction both with and without ancillas: the ancilla-free, cost-optimized layout is a two-row grid, and a $2k$-row layout introduces a space--time tradeoff that cuts depth by $1/k$ while remaining asymptotically optimal for the enlarged register; both are deterministic and analyzed in closed form. The same complexity is also attained on a linear nearest-neighbor chain, so the preservation is topology-independent, holding on any architecture that contains such a chain. All routing bounds are closed-form, giving the concrete resource estimates that heuristic compilers cannot provide at scale.
summary: The paper develops a theoretically optimal method (GPF) for synthesizing diagonal unitary gates. Crucially, it proves that this optimal complexity is maintained when mapping the abstract circuit onto a physically constrained two-dimensional nearest-neighbor grid. This provides essential, closed-form resource estimates that overcome the limitations of heuristic compilation methods.
main_problem: The core problem is developing an asymptotically optimal circuit depth for synthesizing and compiling diagonal unitary operations on quantum hardware constrained by nearest-neighbor connectivity.
main_result: The authors show that the asymptotically optimal depth, $O(2^n/n)$, achieved in all-to-all connectivity using a Gray-Path Framework (GPF), is preserved when compiled onto a two-dimensional nearest-neighbor grid. Furthermore, they detail space-time trade-offs to reduce this depth by factors of $k$.
method: The work combines theoretical circuit synthesis (using recursive decomposition into high/low subspaces) with rigorous compilation techniques that map logical connectivity requirements onto physical 2D lattice movements using offset states and SWAP layers.
model_or_system: The system involves quantum circuits realizing $n$-qubit diagonal unitaries, $\Lambda_n(	heta)$. The target hardware is modeled as a two-dimensional nearest-neighbor grid, with extensions to linear chains. The synthesis relies on the Gray-Path Framework (GPF) structure.
key_observables: Circuit depth ($R_z$ and CNOT layers), gate count, and asymptotic complexity bounds ($\Theta(2^n/n)$).
important_parameters: The number of qubits ($n$), the grid topology (2D nearest-neighbor vs. all-to-all), and the space-time trade-off factor ($k$).
main_assumptions: General-purpose compilers relying on heuristic search are intractable at scale; the analysis assumes the existence of a low-jump Gray code sequence for optimal routing.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the recursive structure of GPF, show the mapping onto the two-row grid using offset states (e.g., Fig. 8), and plot normalized depth/gate count convergence curves demonstrating asymptotic optimality compared to search-based routers.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the optimal synthesis complexity via GPF in all-to-all connectivity, then details the mapping of this structure onto a two-row nearest-neighbor grid using offset states and SWAP layers. Finally, it analyzes depth-space trade-offs by replicating phase layers across additional rows.
why_interesting: This work provides concrete, analytically derived resource estimates for complex quantum operations on realistic hardware architectures, directly addressing the gap between theoretical circuit design and physical implementation constraints relevant to AMO platforms like trapped ions or superconducting qubits.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
